next_question.question: Is the facility secured or unsecured?

notes.note_text: WHY: Whether the facility is secured or unsecured determines which credit score band requirements and whether the loan-to-value check applies.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

A 'secured facility' is defined in Section 2 as a credit facility secured against residential property; an 'unsecured facility' has no security. The product type governs: (a) the minimum credit score band threshold (Section 7); (b) whether the loan-to-value check applies (Section 8 — secured only); and (c) the calculation of the stress-tested rate (Section 9). Accepted values: secured, unsecured.

optimal_path.question: What is the applicant's gross annual income in GBP?

notes.note_text: WHY: Your gross annual income is used to assess whether you meet the minimum income threshold (Route A: £15,000 sole income) and to calculate affordability ratios.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 5(1)(a) (Route A) requires the applicant's gross annual income to be not less than GBP 15,000. 'Gross annual income' is defined in Section 2 as total annual income before tax and deductions. Where the applicant cannot meet Route A alone, Route B (combined income with a joint applicant of at least GBP 20,000) may be used instead — see Section 5(1)(b).

optimal_path.question: What is the applicant's credit score band?

notes.note_text: WHY: Your credit score band determines whether you meet the minimum credit quality requirement. Secured facilities accept fair, good, or excellent; unsecured facilities require good or excellent.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 7(1) sets out the credit score band requirements by product type: (a) for a secured facility, the credit score band must be 'fair', 'good', or 'excellent'; (b) for an unsecured facility, the credit score band must be 'good' or 'excellent'. Section 7(2) states that an applicant with a credit score band of 'poor' or 'very_poor' is not eligible for any product type. The credit score band is determined by a recognised credit reference agency.

optimal_path.question: What is the applicant's employment status?

notes.note_text: WHY: Your employment status determines whether you fall into one of the three eligible categories required under Section 4 of the rules.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 4(1) requires the applicant to be in one of the following employment categories: (a) employed (full-time or part-time); (b) self-employed (trading not less than 2 years); (c) retired (receiving pension income). Section 4(2) explicitly excludes applicants who are unemployed, students, or on zero-hours contracts. Accepted values: employed, self_employed, retired. Not accepted: unemployed, student.

optimal_path.question: Is the applicant an existing Meridian customer (24+ months in good standing)?

notes.note_text: WHY: Existing customers in good standing for 24 months or more are exempt from the debt-to-income ratio requirement under Section 10.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 10(1) provides that an existing customer is exempt from the requirements of Section 6 (debt-to-income ratio). Section 10(2) confirms all other requirements continue to apply. Section 10(3) defines 'good standing' as no missed payments and no adverse events during the 24-month qualifying period. An 'existing customer' is defined in Section 2 as an applicant who has held a Meridian account in good standing for not less than 24 months.

optimal_path.question: Does the applicant have any adverse credit history (CCJ, IVA, bankruptcy, default) in the last 6 years?

notes.note_text: WHY: We must check for adverse credit history because any such record results in an immediate, unconditional refusal under Section 3 of the rules.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 3(1) states: 'An applicant with an adverse credit history must be refused without consideration of any other requirement under these rules.' Section 3(2) defines adverse credit history as any of the following recorded within the preceding 6 years: (a) a County Court Judgment (CCJ) or equivalent; (b) an Individual Voluntary Arrangement (IVA); (c) bankruptcy or sequestration; (d) a default on any credit agreement. This is an absolute disqualification — no waiver, exception, or mitigating factor can override it.

optimal_path.question: Does the applicant pass the affordability stress test?

notes.note_text: WHY: The stress test checks that you could still afford repayments if interest rates were higher than today's rate, as required by Section 9.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 9(1) requires the applicant to demonstrate that monthly repayments remain affordable under a stressed interest rate scenario. Section 9(2) defines the stressed monthly payment using the stress-tested rate (standard variable rate plus 3 percentage points) applied to the full loan amount over the full loan term. Section 9(3) provides that the stressed monthly payment must not exceed 35% of the applicant's gross monthly income.

next_question.question: Did the loss or damage occur within the policy period stated in the endorsement?

notes.note_text: WHY: We need to confirm the loss falls within the covered period before any other clause is considered.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Clause 3(1) of the CAR Policy Defect Exclusion Endorsement Schedule 2025 states: 'This endorsement applies only to loss or damage occurring within the policy period.' Clause 3(2) further provides that where loss or damage occurs outside the policy period, the claim must be refused without consideration of any other clause under this endorsement. This is a threshold gateway: if the loss is outside the period, no further analysis is needed.

optimal_path.question: What category of insured property suffered the loss or damage?

notes.note_text: WHY: Only certain categories of property are covered under this endorsement; plant and equipment is excluded.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Clause 5(1) of the endorsement limits cover to four categories: (a) permanent works; (b) temporary works; (c) existing structures; and (d) materials on site. Clause 5(2) explicitly excludes plant and equipment, which is covered under a separate section of the policy. This is an absolute boundary — no provision of the endorsement can reinstate cover for plant and equipment.

optimal_path.question: Was the damage caused solely in order to gain access to, remove, or replace the defective component?

notes.note_text: WHY: Access damage is re-excluded by Clause 8 after the carve-back, but may be reinstated on large projects under Clause 9.
notes.source: source.md#source/Clause 8: Access and removal damage re-exclusion

notes.note_text:
LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Clause 8(1) re-excludes damage caused solely to gain access to, remove, or replace the defective component, notwithstanding the Clause 7 carve-back. Clause 8(2) defines access damage as damage to property that was not itself defective but was damaged only because it was necessary to remove or disturb it in order to reach the defective component. Where access damage is established, coverage depends on whether Clause 9 enhanced cover applies.

notes.note_text: WHY: We need to confirm the loss falls within the covered period before any other clause is considered.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Clause 3(1) of the CAR Policy Defect Exclusion Endorsement Schedule 2025 states: 'This endorsement applies only to loss or damage occurring within the policy period.' Clause 3(2) further provides that where loss or damage occurs outside the policy period, the claim must be refused without consideration of any other clause under this endorsement. This is a threshold gateway: if the loss is outside the period, no further analysis is needed.

optimal_path.question: Has physical loss of or damage to insured property actually occurred?

notes.note_text: WHY: The endorsement requires both physical loss and a defective component to be established before any claim can proceed.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Clause 4(1) of the endorsement sets out the dual conditions that must both be satisfied: (a) physical loss of or damage to insured property has occurred; and (b) a defective component has been identified in connection with the loss. Clause 4(2) states that a claim which does not establish both physical loss and the presence of a defective component is not within scope. Mere existence of a defect without physical loss is insufficient — Clause 7(3) confirms that property is not to be treated as damaged merely because a defect exists within it.

optimal_path.question: Is this claim for the cost of repairing, replacing, or rectifying the defective component itself?

notes.note_text: WHY: Rectification of the defective component is absolutely excluded — this is the most important filter in the endorsement.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Clause 6(1) absolutely excludes 'the cost of repairing, replacing, or rectifying any component that is itself defective in design, plan, specification, materials, or workmanship.' Clause 6(2) makes clear that this exclusion applies notwithstanding any other provision, including project value, enhanced cover status, and the carve-backs in Clauses 7, 8 and 9. Clause 6(3) confirms no other provision can reinstate rectification cover. This exclusion is absolute and cannot be waived.

optimal_path.question: Was the loss or damage notified to underwriters within 30 days of discovery?

notes.note_text: WHY: Notification within 30 days is a mandatory condition — late notification voids the claim entirely.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Clause 11(1) requires the insured to notify underwriters of any loss or damage within 30 days of discovery. Clause 11(2) states that late notification renders the claim void under this endorsement, notwithstanding satisfaction of all other conditions. There is no discretionary relief from this requirement in the endorsement.

optimal_path.question: Has a defective component been identified in connection with the loss?

notes.note_text: WHY: A defective component must be identified — this is the second mandatory condition of the insuring clause.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Clause 4(1)(b) requires that a defective component has been identified in connection with the loss. A 'defective component' is defined in Clause 2 as any part of the Works that is defective in design, plan, specification, materials, or workmanship. The identification must be in connection with the loss event — a pre-existing known defect in an unrelated part of the Works does not satisfy this condition.

notes.note_text: WHY: The mission type determines whether additional requirements (radiation certificate) apply and whether the age exemption from flight readiness is available.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 7(1) of the Spacecraft Crew Certification Act 2049 requires a valid radiation protection certificate for orbital missions. Section 7(2) confirms no radiation certificate is required for suborbital or lunar missions. Section 6(2) restricts the age exemption for orbital missions (see Section 6 notes). Mission types are defined in Section 2: orbital (one or more complete orbits), suborbital (reaching space but not completing a full orbit), and lunar (to or around the Moon).

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 7(1) of the Spacecraft Crew Certification Act 2049 requires a valid radiation protection certificate for orbital missions. Section 7(2) confirms no radiation certificate is required for suborbital or lunar missions. Section 6(2) restricts the age exemption for orbital missions (see Section 6 notes). Mission types are defined in Section 2: orbital (one or more complete orbits), suborbital (reaching space but not completing a full orbit), and lunar (to or around the Moon).

optimal_path.question: What is the applicant's species?

notes.note_text: WHY: Species eligibility is a hard gate — Vogon nationals are excluded by treaty.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 3(1) of the Spacecraft Crew Certification Act 2049 requires that an applicant must be of an eligible species. Section 3(2) explicitly excludes Vogon nationals by virtue of the Galactic Diplomatic Exclusion Treaty 2045. Section 3(3) provides that where the applicant is a Vogon, the application must be refused without consideration of any other requirement under the Act. Accepted species include: Human, Magrathean, Betelgeusian, and Dolphin.

optimal_path.question: What is the applicant's age?

notes.note_text: WHY: Age determines whether the applicant qualifies for the Section 6 exemption from flight readiness requirements.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 6(1) of the Spacecraft Crew Certification Act 2049 provides that an applicant aged 60 or over is exempt from the flight readiness requirement in Section 4, subject to subsection (2). Section 6(2) removes this exemption where the mission type is 'orbital', unless Section 6(3) applies. Section 6(4)(a) confirms that a senior applicant on a suborbital or lunar mission is exempt; Section 6(4)(b) confirms that a senior applicant on an orbital mission is NOT exempt unless they have 1000+ flight hours.

optimal_path.question: Does the applicant carry a towel at all times during the mission?

notes.note_text: WHY: Carrying a towel is a mandatory requirement under Section 9, in accordance with the Interstellar Hitchhiker Safety Regulations 2042.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 9(1) of the Spacecraft Crew Certification Act 2049 requires the applicant to carry a towel at all times during the mission, in accordance with the Interstellar Hitchhiker Safety Regulations 2042. There are no exceptions or waivers to this requirement. Non-compliance is an absolute bar to certification.

optimal_path.question: What type of propulsion system does the vessel use?

notes.note_text: WHY: The vessel must use an approved propulsion type; Conventional propulsion is not approved for crew certification missions.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 8(1) of the Spacecraft Crew Certification Act 2049 requires the vessel's propulsion system to be of an approved type. Section 8(2) lists the approved types: (a) Infinite Improbability Drive; (b) Bistromathics; and (c) Heart of Gold Special. Section 8(3) explicitly excludes Conventional propulsion. A vessel with a non-listed propulsion system is not approved for crew certification missions.

optimal_path.question: Has the applicant passed a GAA medical examination?

notes.note_text: WHY: Passing a GAA medical examination is Route A for satisfying the medical certification requirement under Section 5.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 5(1)(a) of the Spacecraft Crew Certification Act 2049 (Route A) allows the medical certification requirement to be satisfied by an examination conducted by the Galactic Aviation Authority. Section 5(2) confirms that satisfaction of either Route A or Route B is sufficient. The examination result must be current and within the 730-day validity window established by Section 5A.

optimal_path.question: Is the applicant's medical certificate within 730 days of its date of issue?

notes.note_text: WHY: A medical certificate is only valid for 730 days from its issue date; an expired certificate does not satisfy the medical certification requirement.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 5A(1) of the Spacecraft Crew Certification Act 2049 provides that a medical certificate obtained under Section 5 is valid for 730 days from the date of issue. Section 5A(2) requires that the application date falls within those 730 days; a certificate issued more than 730 days before the application date is expired and does not satisfy the requirement. A new examination or certification must be obtained if the existing certificate has lapsed.

next_question.question: What is the child's age in whole years at the start of the current school year (1 September)?

notes.note_text: WHY: We ask for the child's age to check whether they fall within the compulsory school age range (Reception / age 4 up to, but not including, age 16) that qualifies for free school meals under the Education Act 1996.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 512ZA of the Education Act 1996 prescribes the descriptions of pupils entitled to free school meals under section 512(1)(a). Compulsory school age begins at the start of the term following a child's fifth birthday, but in practice the provision applies from the start of the Reception year (age 4–5).

Regulation 3(1) of the Free School Meals entitlement model states that a person is entitled to a free school lunch if they are a registered pupil at a relevant school in England and are aged under 16. Age is assessed at the start of the school year. A child who turns 16 during the school year is not within scope once the school year has started with them aged 16.

optimal_path.question: What type of school does the child attend — state-funded (maintained school or Academy), independent (fee-paying), or home-educated?

notes.note_text: WHY: Only children attending state-funded schools (maintained schools, Academies, non-maintained special schools, or pupil referral units) are within scope of the free school meals duty. Independent schools and home-educated children are excluded.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:

Section 512ZA of the Education Act 1996 defines 'relevant school' as: (a) a school maintained by a local authority in England; (b) an Academy; (c) a non-maintained special school; (d) a pupil referral unit. Independent schools (fee-paying) and home-educated children are not within scope of this provision.

Section 512ZB(4A)(a) further confirms the requirement that the pupil be 'a registered pupil at a maintained school or pupil referral unit in England'.

The School Standards and Framework Act 1998, section 114, defines 'maintained school' as including community schools, voluntary aided schools, voluntary controlled schools, foundation schools, and community special schools maintained by a local authority in England.
